prs.author: julianknutsen
prs.request:
PR title: feat(beads): proxied-local bd-owned Dolt by default on beads v1.3.0-rc.2

PR description:
## Supported rc.2 migration path

There is exactly one, and it is a command:

```bash
gc stop                                        # mandatory, not hygiene
gc beads city migrate-proxied [--dry-run] [--json] [--rig NAME]
gc doctor --fix && gc doctor                   # backfill what the old init predates
gc start
```

**Preconditions.** A city initialised the legacy GC-managed way: `metadata.json`
`dolt_mode: server` (or no `dolt_mode` at all), `gc.endpoint_origin: managed_city`, one
gc-owned `dolt sql-server` over `<city>/.beads/dolt`, no `.gc/scope-ownership.json` entry.
gc's server must be **stopped**, and the command proves it rather than trusting it: no
published `dolt-state.json`, no live process holding the data-dir lock, nothing listening on
the port in `.beads/dolt-server.port`. That fence is re-checked at the start of every scope's
turn and again immediately before `bd migrate` — bd's own precondition consults only its own
pid file, cannot see a server gc started, and would commit the mode flip onto a data dir Dolt
still holds locked.

**What it does**, per scope, city first (a rig sharing the city's data dir cannot be proxied
while the city is still direct):

1. `dolt init` the **city's** data dir when `.dolt/repo_state.json` is missing — additive,
   beside the existing database directories — and only when the city's own database is in
   there, or the directory is empty.
2. Give a shared-root rig the **relative** `dolt_data_dir` that roots it at the city's data
   dir. Relative is mandatory: beads drops an absolute value on save and `bd migrate` saves
   partway through the flip.
3. Run bd's own `bd migrate from-server-to-proxied-server --idle-timeout 0`.
4. Verify bd's **outcome** — `metadata.json` says `proxied-server`, the in-flight journal is
   gone — not its exit code.
5. Rewrite `.beads/config.yaml` through gc's canonical writer, which is what drops
   `dolt.mode` and gc's managed endpoint keys.
6. Retire gc's own publication: `<scope>/.beads/dolt-server.port`, and for the city the whole
   `.gc/runtime/packs/dolt` pack state. Nothing else comes back for it.
7. `bd ping` the scope.

**Refusals**, all typed, all by name, none of which mutate anything: already proxied
(`already-migrated`, exit 0), embedded, doltlite (recognised by either metadata field),
external endpoint, journaled in `.gc/scope-ownership.json`, already handed to bd by a
committed ownership journal, a rig with its own store *and* a database in the city's dir, a
rig gc cannot place at all, and a city whose data dir holds databases but not its own.

**Rollback story.** There is no reverse migration on rc.2 and this PR does not invent one.
What it gives instead is that **failure is per scope and resumable**: completed scopes stay
migrated, the failed one is reported with its reason, and rerunning the command finishes the
rest — including a rig whose `dolt_data_dir` was written by the run that then failed at
`bd migrate`. Underneath, bd's own migrate journal is what makes a half-finished flip
recoverable; gc verifies that journal is gone before it calls the scope migrated. Going back
further than that means restoring the city from backup.

`--dry-run` prints the exact per-scope plan (every step above, named) and writes nothing.
`--json` is schema'd at `schemas/beads/city/migrate-proxied/result.schema.json`.
Runbook: **`engdocs/runbooks/beads-migrate-proxied.md`**.

## The journaled ownership handoff is NOT in this PR

An earlier revision of this branch carried a hidden `gc dolt-state handoff-inspect` /
`handoff-stop` protocol: bd would spawn gc as a subprocess and take its typed JSON answers as
proof. **That is withdrawn, because bd never calls gc.** bd spawns nothing but `dolt`; it has
no provider, hook or callback into its caller; everything it needs about the caller arrives as
command-line input. A transfer built the other way makes bd's ownership journal depend on a
binary it cannot verify and makes gc's refusals reachable only through bd.

When the handoff lands it will be **gc-orchestrated over bd verbs** — a phased, journal-driven
`bd migrate ownership-handoff` (`prepare` → `legacy-gone` → `configure` → `verify` → `commit`,
with `rollback`/`rollback-finish` and a non-mutating `status`), with bd owning the journal, the
replacement server, the fences and the rollback, and gc stopping and restarting only its own
legacy server in between. No beads tag has those verbs, so gc ships no driver for one.

What this PR **keeps** is the reading half, which that design still needs: the committed-journal
projection and the three-arm provider-ownership classification, so a scope bd has taken over is
recognised as bd's the moment such a journal exists. On rc.2 nothing writes one, and gc never
will — it is bd's record of bd's own transfer.

Also gone with the protocol: the `gc.json.raw_protocol` cobra annotation, which had no other
user, and the strict managed-stop identity arm, which no non-protocol caller ever passed an
identity to.

## Summary

On beads `v1.3.0-rc.2`, a **fresh** `gc init` with no transport selector now produces a
**bd-owned proxied-local store**: bd runs a `db-proxy-child` supervising a `dolt sql-server`
under `<scope>/.beads/dolt`, and Gas City never starts a Dolt process of its own for that
scope. `gc doctor`, `gc bd`, `gc rig add`, `gc start`, `gc status` and `gc stop` all work
against it, on Linux, proven end to end against the real rc.2 binary.

What changes for a fresh city:

- **bd owns the lifecycle.** `.beads/metadata.json` `dolt_mode: proxied-server` is the
  topology authority. Gas City keeps only `.gc/scope-ownership.json` as a crash-safe
  *intent* journal (`provider_initializing` → `ready`). No second topology store.
- **The proxy is pinned resident.** GC-owned proxied scopes initialise with
  `--proxied-server-idle-timeout 0` (sidecar `idle_timeout: -1`); without it eve [truncated]

prs.title: feat(mail,supervisor): send one notification per condition, not one per interval
prs.author: sjarmak
prs.request:
PR title: feat(mail,supervisor): send one notification per condition, not one per interval

PR description:
## What broke

A repeating notifier re-detects the same condition on every run. Both notifiers in
this tree mailed on every detection.

The Dolt store-maintenance loop sent one `[ALERT]` per failed cycle:

```go
	if run.Err != "" {
		m.sendFailureAlert(run)
	}
```

So a store that stays broken mails the operator once per interval, forever, and
nothing at all marks the moment it starts working again. The signal that matters (the
state changed) is buried in the signal that does not (it is still in that state).

Orders that notify through `gc mail send` had the same problem with no way to express
it: the command sends unconditionally, so a patrol that re-detects a condition every
run either floods the mailbox or keeps its own side state.

## The fix, part one: a dedup capability for mail

`mail` gains one optional provider capability:

```go
type DedupSender interface {
	SendDeduped(from, to, subject, body, key string) (msg Message, suppressed bool, err error)
}
```

`beadmail` implements it with a single metadata-keyed list: if a live message with the
same key is already in the same mailbox, that message is returned with
`suppressed=true` and nothing is created. A probe error fails the send rather than
risking a silent duplicate. Providers that cannot query their own history do not
implement the interface, and callers fall back to a plain send, because a duplicate
notification beats a dropped one.

"Same mailbox" is the inbox's own question, not a string comparison. An alias and the
session id behind it resolve to one mailbox in `Inbox`, so the probe matches the stored
assignee against every route that resolves to the recipient. A stream that addresses
one mailbox both ways gets one live copy, not two.

`gc mail send --dedup <key>` exposes it and exits 0 when suppressed.

The dedup horizon is deliberately the previous message's live lifetime. The probe reads
only open messages and archiving closes one, so an archived notification no longer
matches and the stream may alert again. A sender that wants a longer re-alert cadence
keeps its own last-sent state; this is the cheap case, not a general scheduler.

`Provider.Archive`'s own doc comment claimed it deleted the message bead. It closes it,
and the comment now says so.

## The fix, part two: one alert per condition in the maintenance loop

The loop does not use the dedup capability, because it already holds state across runs.
It keys alerts on a stage-plus-error fingerprint and mails only when that changes: once
on entering a failure, again if the failure changes shape mid-streak, and once on
recovery. The recovery notice is new, and it carries how long the failure ran and how
many repeats were suppressed. The state is in memory, so a supervisor restart re-alerts
a still-broken store exactly once, which doubles as a liveness reminder rather than
silence.

Three things about that are less obvious than the happy path, and each of them is the
difference between a useful alert and a misleading one.

**What the loop observes and what the operator knows are different.** A mail backend
that is down must not cost the streak. The fingerprint follows the failure the store is
actually in and advances even when the send fails; a separate flag says whether that
alert got out. Suppressing a repeat needs both, so an undelivered alert is retried by
the next identical run instead of reading as a repeat of something never received, and
a failure whose alert was lost is still the failure the recovery notice names, with a
line saying the notice is the first the operator has seen of it. A recovery notice that
cannot be sent is owed rather than dropped, and that owed state is tracked too: without
it, a store that recovers and breaks the same way again matches the retained
fingerprint and is suppressed as a repeat of an outage that had already ended. A
failure arriving with a notice still owed clears the lot and opens a new outage.

**The error text is part of the contract.** Because the fingerprint is the rendered
error, a failure message carrying a per-run value reads as a new condition every cycle
and the suppression is worth nothing. One did: the snapshot stage wrapped `os.Rename`'s
`*os.LinkError` verbatim, and that renders the destination path, whose leaf is the run's
own timestamp. It now names the destination directory and wraps the errno underneath,
so `errors.Is` still reaches it and the text holds still. Text that an external backup
or SQL backend varies per attempt is outside the loop's control and will re-alert.

**A skipped cycle is not a success.** A disk-critical pre-flight skips the snapshot and
`CALL DOLT_GC` and finishes with no error. Read as a success, it closes an open alert
with a recovery notice for a store nothing has touched, which is the opposite of what an
operator needs while the disk is full. The alert state machine is simply not consulted
for it: the skip is the one completion path that records its event and stops there, which
keeps the fact where it is used instead of on `MaintenanceRun`, a value the status and
trigger APIs project onto the wire. The `gc.store.maintenance.done` event a skipped cycle
emits is long-standing behavior and unchanged here; `StoreDiskCritical` is what tells
operators why the cycle skipped.

Two smaller ones: `Failing since` names the run that opened the outage rather than the
run where the failure last changed shape, because an operator reads that line as the
length of the outage; and the suppressed-repeat count stays per shape, with the line it
prints on saying so.

## Lock discipline

`emitRunEvent` now mutates mu-guarded alert state, so it is renamed
`emitRunEventLocked` to say so, and the three pre-existing test call sites go through
the same locked helper the new tests use. Holding the lock across the alert send is not
new contention: it is the cycle lease, already held for the whol [truncated]

PR description:
## What

#5816 (p2) has three asks. This addresses only the narrow, mechanical one: an operator CLI verb to drop a stale pending nudge, replacing manual `.gc/nudges/state.json` surgery. The other two — auto-detecting an epoch-superseded nudge against a continuously-busy target (the existing fence check only runs inside the delivery-attempt path, which requires session idleness, so it never fires against a busy session), and a TTL/expiry policy — are genuine design decisions (what's a "safe" wait, configurable or not, drop-vs-redeliver-as-default) and are explicitly not addressed here.

## Fix

`gc nudge drop <id>...` (matches the existing `gc mail delete <id>...` multi-ID convention), `--json` supported. Classifies each ID against current queue state, then calls the existing `recordQueuedNudgeFailureWithStore`/`failedQueuedNudge` dead-letter path in one batch — the same machinery `status`/`drain` already exercise internally on a real delivery failure, so a dropped nudge lands in the identical terminal state. No new state-machine logic.

One implementation detail: `failedQueuedNudge` only forces *immediate* dead-letter (vs. requeue-with-retry-delay) for a cause satisfying `errors.Is(cause, errNudgeSessionFenceMismatch)`. Rather than touching that function's branching, the new drop cause implements the standard `Is(target error) bool` method to report equivalence to that sentinel — idiomatic `errors.Is` usage, `failedQueuedNudge` itself is untouched, and the stored `LastError` text still reads "dropped by operator (gc nudge drop)" rather than borrowing the fence-mismatch sentinel's own message.

Per-ID outcomes are distinguished (droppable → dead-lettered, already-dead → clear no-op, not-found → clear error) and a batch with mixed valid/invalid IDs still processes the valid ones.

## Follow-up fixes included in this PR

prs.title: feat(reconciler): emit a counted event when a control scope has no dispatcher
prs.author: julianknutsen
prs.request:
PR title: feat(reconciler): emit a counted event when a control scope has no dispatcher

PR description:
Rebased onto `main`; the former #5918 dependency is already upstream. The scope-gap event and its tests remain, with generated Go and dashboard clients refreshed.

## Problem

`repairControlDispatcherRoutesForStoreScope` suppresses a control row whose owning scope configures no control-dispatcher — routing it to another scope's dispatcher would park it on a store that dispatcher cannot read — and reports the gap by printing one stderr line per scope.

The "report once" budget lives on the per-pass repair object, and `buildDesiredState` rebuilds that object every tick. So a standing config gap does not report once: it reports once per scope **per tick**, forever. On maintainer-city that was 600+ identical lines over 26h with every health surface green, and the stall behind them was found by reading them by hand (ga-oytw9). The line also names ONE bead per scope, so one stuck row and a hundred read identically.

## Change

The repair pass now returns a typed summary per scope — the label the stderr line already prints, the owning rig context, the leg the rows were collected through, the count of rows it suppressed, and one sample bead — carried out on `DesiredStateResult.ControlDispatcherScopeGaps`. `CityRuntime.buildDesiredState` turns each entry into one `control.dispatcher_scope_gap` event, so the condition reaches `gc events`, the dashboard and alerting instead of only whoever greps controller stderr. The stderr line is unchanged, for trace readers that already grep it.

Three decisions worth reviewing:

- **Emitted at the FRESH build, not where the result is consumed.** `loadDemandSnapshot` reuses a cached result across stable patrol ticks, so a consumer-side emission would replay an observation that tick never made. Emitting inside `cr.buildDesiredState` covers both fresh-build call sites (startup and the demand snapshot) and keeps each event one-for-one with the stderr line the same build printed.
- **One event per scope, level-triggered.** The gap is a property of the city's config, not of any one bead, so a subscriber reads the current count rather than summing a history.
- **`control.dispatcher_scope_gap`, not `control_dispatcher.scope_gap`.** The design suggested the latter shape; every event type already in the registry spells its domain as a single word, with underscores only in the action segment (`session.demand_claim_divergence`, `control.stalled`). This extends the `control.*` vocabulary `control.stalled` opened rather than adding the first underscore-bearing domain. Say the word if you want the literal design spelling instead.

A misaligned index-aligned input returns no gaps at all: it suppresses every control route without evaluating a single scope, so reporting that blanket suppression as a config finding would be a fabrication. It keeps its own existing diagnostic.

The typed payload is registered next to `ControlStalledPayload` in `internal/events`, so the SSE union, the OpenAPI spec and the generated Go/TS clients pick it up. Those artifacts (`internal/api/openapi.json`, `docs/reference/schema/openapi.{json,txt}`, `internal/api/genclient/client_gen.go`, the dashboard's generated client and `dist/`) are regenerated in this commit.

## Tests

RED→GREEN, in order:

| Test | RED evidence |
| --- | --- |
| `TestEveryKnownEventTypeHasRegisteredPayload` (`internal/api`) | The constant landed before the payload: `unregistered event types: [control.dispatcher_scope_gap]` |
| `TestControlDispatcherScopeGapIsAKnownEventTypeWithATypedPayload`, `TestControlDispatcherScopeGapPayloadRoundTrips` (`internal/events`) | `undefined: ControlDispatcherScopeGapPayload` |
| `TestBuildDesiredState_ReportsControlDispatcherScopeGapForRigRootedWork`, `TestRepairControlDispatcherRoutesCountsSuppressedRowsPerScope`, `TestRepairControlDispatcherRoutesReportsNoScopeGapWhenDispatcherIsConfigured` (`cmd/gc`) | `result.ControlDispatcherScopeGaps undefined` |
| `TestEmitControlDispatcherScopeGapEvents_*`, `TestCityRuntimeBuildDesiredStateRecords*` (`cmd/gc`) | `undefined: emitControlDispatcherScopeGapEvents` |

Coverage: the class-binding fixture with only a city dispatcher now also asserts one gap entry naming the binding and the owning rig with a count of 1; two rows of one scope collapse to one entry with count 2; a scope that HAS a dispatcher reports none, so a healthy city stays silent. On the runtime side, a `CityRuntime` whose build reports a gap records exactly one typed event keyed on the owning scope ref (`rig:fixture` / `city:<name>`, never the class-binding leg — a subscriber keying on the leg could not tell two rigs' gaps apart), a build with no gap records nothing, and a nil recorder does not panic.

**Mutation probe:** replacing the `emitControlDispatcherScopeGapEvents(...)` call in `cr.buildDesiredState` with `_ = emitControlDispatcherScopeGapEvents` leaves every build-side test green and fails only `TestCityRuntimeBuildDesiredStateRecordsControlDispatcherScopeGapEvents` (`recorded events = [], want one control.dispatcher_scope_gap`).

## Gates

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./cmd/gc ./internal/events ./internal/api`, `gofmt -l`, `golangci-lint run ./cmd/gc/... ./internal/events/...`, `./scripts/check-residency-boundary.sh`, `go test ./internal/events/... ./cmd/gc -run 'ControlDispatcher|ScopeGap|Event'`, `TestOpenAPISpecInSync` / `TestGeneratedClientInSync`, `make dashboard-ci`, `make test-fast-parallel` — all clean.

prs.title: fix(tmux): back off the process snapshot instead of re-forking it every refresh
prs.author: remuscazacu
prs.request:
PR title: fix(tmux): back off the process snapshot instead of re-forking it every refresh

PR description:
## The loop

The full-OS `ps` scan behind the tmux state cache fails by losing a CPU race: the box is saturated, the scan does not finish inside the 3s `fetchTimeout`, and the context kills it (`signal: killed`).

`FetchState` degrades rather than erroring — it keeps the authoritative tmux liveness and marks process detail unavailable. That is correct and deliberate, and this PR does not change it.

The consequence is that `refresh()` books the fetch as a **success**: it stamps `fetchedAt`, clears `dirty`, and has no way to know the expensive half just died. Nothing remembers the failure, so the very next refresh re-forks the same full-OS scan into the same contention that just starved it. A loaded box keeps paying `fetchTimeout` plus a whole-process-table scan for a probe that cannot succeed while it stays loaded — and the paying is part of why it stays loaded.

## Observed

A 4-core / 15.7 GB workstation running two cities and seven rigs, supervisor up 7d10h:

- `process snapshot degraded` **74/hr** — one futile scan every ~48s
- load average 17–22, 0.0% idle, every liveness probe failing
- the probe never recovered on its own; only a supervisor restart cleared it
- stopping the supervisor dropped load to 3.96 and idle to 81%, attributing it to this process rather than to the other tenants on the box

## The change

A gate on `tmuxFetcher` bounds re-attempts: 15s after the first failure, doubling to a 2 minute cap, cleared on the first success. While closed, `FetchState` skips the scan and returns the same degraded answer it would otherwise have spent `fetchTimeout` to reach.

- **Silent while skipping** — a line per skip would only move the cost from CPU to the log.
- **Recovery logged once**, not on every healthy refresh thereafter.
- **The degrade log now names the window**, so the backoff is visible where the failure already was.

It does not weaken the answer. A failed snapshot already degrades optimistically in `processAlive`, on the rule that a failed secondary probe must never trigger a reap or respawn. Holding that state longer is the same answer held longer, while the machine gets back the CPU that lets the next attempt finish.

The gate lives on `tmuxFetcher` rather than `StateCache` because the cache cannot see this failure at all — by the time `refresh()` looks, the degrade has already been rendered as a success. Its zero value attempts immediately, so the several `&tmuxFetcher{tm: tm}` literals across the package and its tests behave exactly as before.

## Tests

New `state_cache_snapshot_backoff_test.go`: zero value allows; window opens/closes on schedule; doubling to the cap; success clears and reports recovery exactly once; `FetchState` skips the scan while gated **and retains session liveness**; a skipped snapshot degrades optimistically like a failed one.

`go test ./internal/runtime/tmux/` passes, `go vet` clean, `golangci-lint run ./internal/runtime/tmux/...` reports 0 issues.

PR description:
## What

Closes #5845. The controller and wake sockets both already fall back to a sha256-hashed `/tmp` path when their canonical `.gc/*.sock` path would exceed the ~104-108 byte Unix domain socket path limit (macOS/Linux respectively) — the supervisor socket had no equivalent guard, so a long `GC_HOME`/`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` fails the bind with an opaque `bind: invalid argument` instead of falling back like its two siblings.

## Fix

A one-to-one copy of the existing `controllerSocketPathLimit`/`wakeSocketPathLimit` pattern: `supervisorSocketPathLimit = 100`, falling back to `/tmp/gascity-supervisor/<sha256(dir)[:16]>.sock` when the canonical path exceeds it. The existing `guardSupervisorSocketDir(dir)` call is unchanged.

New tests (`cmd_supervisor_test.go`): short dir unchanged (regression guard), long dir falls back correctly, fallback is deterministic per-dir, and two different long dirs don't collide (needed since `supervisorSocketPathCandidates()` feeds both a live and default path).

While validating this change against the full local test suite, two pre-existing tests — `TestRunSupervisorWarnsOnEphemeralAPIPort` and `TestRunSupervisorNoWarningForLowAPIPort` — started hanging indefinitely. PR title: fix(doctor): pin custom-types checks to configured store

PR description:
## Summary

- Resolve the custom-types probe's Beads store from the selected city or rig scope.
- Use the same scoped environment for CSV reads, registered-type reads, and repair writes.
- Clear ambient backend, endpoint, database, data-directory, socket, and shared-server selectors while preserving authentication helpers.
- Add a two-server regression test that proves a poisoned ambient environment cannot redirect reads or repairs to a decoy store.

Fixes #4896.

## Why

`gc doctor` previously set only the subprocess working directory before invoking `bd`. A developer's ambient `GC_DOLT_*`, `BEADS_DOLT_SERVER_*`, backend, database, or shared-server variables could therefore override the store configured for the selected scope. The probe could report missing custom types for the wrong store, and `--fix` could write to that wrong store.

This change resolves the configured store once and projects that context explicitly into every `bd` subprocess used by the check.

## Testing

- [x] `go test -count=1 ./internal/doctor`
- [x] `go test -count=1 ./internal/testpolicy/resourcecensus`
- [x] `go vet ./internal/doctor ./internal/testpolicy/resourcecensus`
- [x] `go test -count=1 -run '^$' ./cmd/gc`
- [ ] `make check` — the pinned linter started successfully, but the local Go compiler exhausted the machine's remaining temporary disk space while type-checking Dolt. No lint finding was emitted before the infrastructure failure; CI should run the complete gate.
- [ ] `make check-docs` — the documentation test reached its link step, but the linker hit the same local disk-capacity failure. CI should run the complete gate.
- [ ] `make test-integration` — the behavior is covered by the focused live two-server regression test.

## Long-term prevention

This PR intentionally keeps the fix narrow. A follow-up direction is to make one rule explicit across Gas City:

> Resolve store context at the scope boundary, project it explicitly, and never inherit store-selection state from the ambient process.

Concretely:

1. Represent every `gc` to `bd` boundary with one scoped store context: scope root, backend, endpoint, database, authentication reference, and transport.
2. Generate both shell-out and native-open configuration from that resolved context, with credentials explicitly allowlisted and redacted from diagnostics.
3. Add a shared hostile-environment test matrix for embedded, managed-local, explicit external, and inherited-rig stores. Each case should prove that reads and writes reach only the selected store.
4. Extend `gc doctor` provenance output to show the selected scope and redacted configuration sources, including which ambient selectors were ignored.

The two-server test in this PR is the first narrow sentinel for that policy; it does not introduce a new public configuration model.

## Checklist

- [x] Linked an issue.
- [x] Added tests for the behavior change.
- [x] No user-facing documentation change is required for this corrective behavior. [truncated]

`setCustomTypes` set `cmd.Dir` but leave `cmd.Env` unset, so the `bd`
subprocess inherits `os.Environ()` including any ambient `BEADS_DOLT_SERVER_*`
/ `GC_DOLT_*`:

```go
func getCustomTypes(dir string) ([]string, error) {
	...
	cmd := exec.Command("bd", args...)
	cmd.Dir = dir
	out, err := cmd.Output()   // inherits ambient BEADS_DOLT_SERVER_* → wrong server
	...

```

`gc bd` does **not** have this problem: its subprocess env is built by

prs.title: feat(doctor): warn when the managed Dolt server log grows unbounded
prs.author: Rome-1
prs.request:
PR title: feat(doctor): warn when the managed Dolt server log grows unbounded

PR description:
## Problem

`dolt.log` is opened `O_APPEND` at every managed server start and is never truncated or rotated.

Nothing in the repo bounds it:

- The rotation in `internal/events` (`WithMaxSize`, `ForceRotate`) is wired to `.gc/events.jsonl` only.
- No maintenance order or restart path trims it — `dolt_start_managed.go` and the legacy shell fallback both append, and stop/restart only `tail`/`wc -c` the file for offset tracking.
- No doctor check references `dolt.log` at all. `EventLogSizeCheck` covers `events.jsonl`, `BdBackupSizeCheck` covers `.beads/backup/`, `DoltNomsSizeCheck` and `DoltJournalSizeCheck` cover the data directory. The server log has no canary.

It also grows faster than the absence of a bound suggests. The server reaps abandoned client connections at the `wait_timeout` boundary and logs one ERROR per reap, which on one managed city came to **21 MB in a single day with nothing failing** — the reaper working as designed, logged at error severity. (#5871 removes that particular source at the pool; this PR bounds the file regardless of what writes to it.)

This class of unbounded growth has already caused an incident here: #3897, where `supervisor.log` reached 645 MB during a crash loop. That fix was never generalized to the server log.

## What this adds

A `dolt-log-size` doctor check, following the `dolt-journal-size` template:

- Same managed-Dolt applicability gate, so file-backed and external-endpoint workspaces are not warned about a file they do not have.
- Same env-overridable thresholds — `GC_DOLT_LOG_WARN_BYTES` (default 512 MB) and `GC_DOLT_LOG_ERROR_BYTES` (default 2 GB). An invalid value falls back to the default rather than silently disabling the canary, and there is a test for that.
- Resolves the log path the same way `cmd/gc` does when it starts the server: `GC_DOLT_LOG_FILE` wins, otherwise `dolt.log` in the pack state directory. One test deliberately exercises the default path rather than the env override, so a layout change cannot quietly make every other case measure a file the server never writes.

`doltJournalThreshold` is renamed `doltEnvByteThreshold` now that a second check reads byte thresholds from the environment through it. No behavior change.

## Why a canary and not rotation

The repo has already taken a position on unbounded files: surface the size, let the operator pick the cleanup. `BdBackupSizeCheck` says so in its own `CanFix` comment.

`CanFix` is false here for a further reason. Truncating in place is safe against a live `O_APPEND` writer, but discarding the log destroys the only record of why the server behaved as it did, and whether to archive first is operator policy. The check reports the size and the path; the operator picks the recipe.

Happy to follow up with real rotation instead if you would rather have that — it is a larger change and a different review.

## Testing

- 10 new tests in `internal/doctor/checks_dolt_log_size_test.go` covering the skip flag, the applicability gate, a missing log, the default-path resolver, warn and error thresholds, env overrides, an invalid env value, a non-regular file, and `CanFix`.
- `go vet ./internal/doctor/ ./cmd/gc/` clean.
- Full `internal/doctor` package suite green.

PR title: fix(nudge): re-fence stale queued nudges instead of dead-lettering (ga-bow)

PR description:
## Problem and fix

When a session is re-created after a failed spawn (a fresh wake bumps the
ContinuationEpoch; a re-materialization can mint a new SessionID),
splitQueuedNudgesForTarget was routing every fence-mismatched item into
recordQueuedNudgeFailureWithStore with errNudgeSessionFenceMismatch,
which failedQueuedNudge treats as a permanent dead-letter. That was
whole-queue data loss on every incarnation flip: 12 nudges (including
--delivery immediate) died on one refinery respawn in thunderfartcity.

The claim path (queuedNudgeClaimableForTarget) already validates seat
identity via matchesQueueAgent — items only reach split because this
seat owns them, so a stale SessionID/ContinuationEpoch just marks the
prior incarnation of the same seat. Re-fence in memory onto the current
target's fence and hand the items back as deliverable; the caller drains
them into one coalesced delivery to the live incarnation. Targets with
no resolved sessionID still reject (nothing to re-fence to), preserving
the invariant that fenced items are not delivered to an unresolved
target.

Refs ga-bow, thunderfartcity:gp-u63s.



## Testing

New coverage pins the re-fence path: fence-mismatched queued nudges are re-fenced to the live incarnation instead of dead-lettered, and genuinely unroutable items still dead-letter. Nudge suite green; merged through the fork's full pre-push gate.

PR description:
## Summary

Fixes #5900. A `graph.v2` workflow root's `gc.run_target` claim fallback
(added for #2763 so a genuinely root-only molecule is claimable as its own
unit of work) did not distinguish that shape from a **fully-expanded** root

Since the root→finalize edge is deliberately non-blocking (`tracks`, not
`blocks` — see `addWorkflowRootDeps`), the root goes dependency-ready in that
window and the fallback let it be claimed anyway, even though
`WorkflowTopologyKinds` documents workflow roots as never-claimable. Pool
workers then repeatedly claimed and drained the unclosable root (observed: 0
closures over ~2 hours against a `luna-worker`-routed root).

expansion state at **compile time** rather than reading child count at claim
time:

prs.title: fix(doltpool): bound idle connections below the server's wait_timeout
prs.author: Rome-1
prs.request:
PR title: fix(doltpool): bound idle connections below the server's wait_timeout

PR description:
## What

Adds `db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(20 * time.Second)` to the shared Dolt pool.

## Why

`internal/doltpool` sets `maxIdleConns = 2` and `connMaxLifetime = time.Hour`, but no idle timeout. An idle pooled connection therefore lives up to an hour, while gc's own managed Dolt config sets the server's `wait_timeout` to **30 seconds**. The server reaps the connection first and logs an error for each one:

```
Error reading packet from client N: read tcp ... i/o timeout
io.ReadFull(header size) failed
```

On one managed city this produced **6565 ERROR lines in a single day**, continuous from 00:00 to 17:22. The timestamps land on seconds `:02`, `:28`, `:32`, `:58` — two interleaved series on a 30s cycle, matching `wait_timeout` exactly. `ss` attribution showed every connection belonged to `gc`, with the churn concentrated on the supervisor's reconcile loop.

Nothing is failing here: this is the reaper working as designed, logged at ERROR. The costs are that a log crying wolf thousands of times a day trains operators to discount it, and the server burns CPU managing sockets the client should have closed itself.

## Why this value

`SetConnMaxIdleTime` must sit **strictly below** `wait_timeout` so the client closes idle connections first, removing the events at the source rather than muting them. 20s leaves a 10s margin; equality with `wait_timeout` would be a race, not a bound.

`connMaxLifetime` is deliberately left at an hour — it bounds connection *age*, not idleness, and age is not what the server is reaping.

This follows the lineage of the package itself, which was introduced to eliminate per-operation Open+Close churn (its own comment cites 2,618 TIME_WAIT sockets from one call site). This is the same class of problem one level down: connections that outlive what the other end expects.

## Not included

The log **severity** is not addressed here. `Error reading packet from client` is emitted by Dolt's go-mysql-server, so it is not this project's to change; it would be a separate issue upstream. Bundling the two would stall the half that can actually land.

## Test

`go build`, `go vet`, and `go test ./internal/doltpool/` all pass.

   the HTTP/dashboard-facing API server path) — wires a live recorder:
   `Recorder: s.state.EventProvider()`.
2. **`cmd/gc/worker_handle.go:79-90`**
   (`workerFactoryWithStaleKeyDetectionWaiter`, the *only*
   `worker.Factory` constructor `cmd/gc` uses) — builds
   `worker.FactoryConfig{...}` with **no `Recorder` field set at all**.
   Every CLI-driven session-lifecycle helper in `cmd/gc` funnels through
   this factory (`workerHandleForSessionWithConfig`,
   `workerHandleForSessionTargetWithConfig`,
   `workerKillSessionTargetWithConfig`,
   `workerStopSessionTargetWithConfig`,
   `workerInterruptSessionTargetWithConfig`,
   `workerRespondSessionTargetWithConfig`, plus the session-catalog/
   session-new paths in `cmd/gc/cmd_session.go`).

The comment already at `operation_events.go:256-262` names this precisely:
usage facts still flow on CLI-factory handles because they get a sink but
"no event recorder (the CLI factory path)" — but it means CLI-driven
session lifecycle (start/attach/create/stop/kill/interrupt/message/nudge/
respond/close/rename) silently never emits `worker.operation` for any
session managed via the `gc` CLI/controller surface rather than the HTTP
API server.

A live `events.Provider` is already available in-process to the CLI/
controller code — `controllerState.EventProvider()`
(`cmd/gc/api_state.go:1475`), already used elsewhere in `cmd/gc` (e.g.
`cmd/gc/route_recovery.go:59-63`, `cmd/gc/city_runtime.go:3646`) — it is
simply never threaded into `worker.FactoryConfig.Recorder` at the CLI
factory construction site.

## Impact

Any city that runs its session lifecycle through the `gc` CLI/controller
surface rather than the HTTP API server (e.g. supervisor-managed pool/
manager/worker sessions) never gets `worker.operation` events for that
lifecycle, so `gc analyze reliability` skips ~100% of lifecycle events with
"instrumentation gap," and any tooling depending on `worker.operation` for
CLI-driven sessions is blind. This likely also underlies part of the
symptom in #3928 (session lifecycle events missing from the event stream),
though that issue is scoped to `session.*` event types generally and to
`start-pending` wedge detection — this issue is the specific root cause for
the `worker.operation` non-emission piece.

## Fix candidates

1. Thread a live `events.Recorder` (sourced from
   `controllerState.EventProvider()` or equivalent) into
   `worker.FactoryConfig.Recorder` at `cmd/gc/worker_handle.go:79-90`
   (`workerFactoryWithStaleKeyDetectionWaiter`), mirroring
   `internal/api/worker_factory.go:21`. This is a call-site fix — the
   emitter and gating logic are already correct; only the CLI factory's
   struct literal needs the field set.
2. Default `worker.FactoryConfig.Recorder` (or `NewFactory`/
   `handle_construct.go`) to a shared process-wide recorder instead of
   `events.Discard` when no explicit recorder is supplied, so any future
   factory construction site gets live recording by default rather than
   requiring every caller to remember to wire it.

Candidate 1 is the more surgical fix and matches the existing pattern at
the API server call site; candidate 2 closes the gap for any *future*
factory construction site as well but changes default behavior more
broadly.

## Repro

```
$ gc analyze reliability
506 lifecycle event(s) dropped before grouping (skipped + ambiguous_aliases).
506 lifecycle event(s) skipped: no worker.operation observed for the session
at or before the event (instrumentation gap).
```

An argv the scanner cannot parse (an unrecognized flag whose value consumption is undecidable) is forwarded untouched rather than guessed at.

prs.title: fix(events): fail a short single-record write instead of counting it as written
prs.author: rjgeng
prs.request:
PR title: fix(events): fail a short single-record write instead of counting it as written

PR description:
`internal/events/recorder.go` has two write paths and only one checks its byte count. `writeBatch` returns `io.ErrShortWrite` when it writes fewer bytes than it was given. `writeRecordLocked` — the single-record path behind `Record()` and the rotation anchor write — discarded the count and kept only the error, so a short write that returned a nil error committed a partial line, incremented `recordCount`, and left the already-bumped `seq` in place. The recorder treated it as a complete record and appended everything after it behind the fragment.

Nothing detected that and nothing reported it. A partial line is indistinguishable from a torn write to every downstream reader, which is the corrupted-tail shape the recorder's startup truncation has to repair — so this and #5614 compose: truncation removes the damage, this stops the single-record path from producing it silently.

**Credit:** @sjarmak spotted this asymmetry while reviewing #5614 and noted it was "plausibly one source of the corruption being repaired here." That is exactly what it looks like from here.

**Fix:** route the single-record write through `writeBatch` so both paths get the guard from one implementation rather than two copies of the same check. The marshal-and-write step moves into `encodeAndWriteRecord`, which takes an `io.Writer` — `FileRecorder.file` is a concrete `*os.File`, so there was previously no way to inject a short writer and cover this path at all. The new test reuses the `shortBatchWriter` helper already in the package.

**Testing:** full `./internal/events` package green; `gofmt` and `golangci-lint --new-from-rev=origin/main --whole-files` clean; pre-commit hook passed in full. Red-green confirmed — with the guard reverted the new test fails with `error = <nil>, want io.ErrShortWrite`.

Does not conflict with #5614; verified by test merge, either order works.

prs.title: fix(config): make model and effort open options across all providers (ga-fyh)
prs.author: brandonmartin
prs.request:
PR title: fix(config): make model and effort open options across all providers (ga-fyh)

PR description:
Fixes the class of defect where a `model` or `effort` pin that gc cannot honor is **silently discarded** instead of erroring — the agent then runs the provider CLI's default, unpinned, with no warning.

## Why

`internal/worker/builtin/profiles.go` carried a hand-maintained `Choices` enum per provider. A value absent from that enum has no `FlagArgs`, so the launch path emits no `--model` at all, while the named-session resolution path hard-errors on the same value. The two paths disagree and the launch path fails open.

This was live in a running city: `gasburger.refinery` and `gasburger.gorkcats` pinned `model = "grok-4.6"`, which was not in the grok enum (`grok-build`, `grok-composer-2.5`, `grok-composer-2.5-fast`). Confirmed from process args:

    grok --permission-mode bypassPermissions --effort high

No `--model`. Both agents had been running the grok CLI default rather than the pinned model, silently.

The same defect class was fixed for Claude on 2026-08-03 in 41d35b765 (#4739/#4740) after incident ra-jbbv0 — that fix added canonical `claude-*` ids but did not generalize, so every other provider kept the hole. The grok enum had not been touched since cf69ca5d6 (2026-06-07), the commit that first added the provider.

## Scope — `effort` too, not just `model`

An audit of all 20 provider profiles found the effort axis equally broken:

- 13 providers have **no** effort option at all — every `effort =` pin silently dropped
- 7 (kiro, cursor, copilot, amp, zcode, auggie, omp) have **neither** model nor effort
- `effort = "max"` on **codex** is dropped (its enum stops at `xhigh`) even though claude's `OptionDefaults` ships `"max"` — the value looks blessed but isn't portable
- **antigravity** drops `xhigh` and `max`

## Design note carried in the change

Effort is not universally a separate flag. **cursor** and **antigravity** encode it *inside* the model id (`claude-opus-5-low`, `gemini-3.6-flash-high`), and cursor adds an orthogonal `-fast` axis. `cursor-agent --list-models` returns 198 models against zero in gc's cursor profile. So `(model, effort)` must resolve per-provider, sometimes composing into a single string — a registry that assumes a separate `--effort` flag everywhere would mis-handle both.

## Bead trail

- `ga-fyh` — this work
- `ga-cot` — cursor catalog catch-up, dep-blocked on this landing
- `ga-psh` — this PR
